title: Checkout latency spikes every night at 01:00 (a noisy neighbour)
intro: Every night around 01:00, checkout's p99 latency jumps from 80ms to 2s for about 40 minutes. Checkout's code and traffic don't change at that time. Only some checkout pods are affected.

steps.prompt: See which nodes the checkout pods (app=checkout, namespace shop) run on.
expected_commands: kubectl get pods -n shop -l app=checkout -o wide
kubectl get po -n shop -l app=checkout -o wide
steps.fake_output:
NAME                        READY   STATUS    NODE
checkout-5d7c8b6a4-a1b2c    1/1     Running   node-3
checkout-5d7c8b6a4-d3e4f    1/1     Running   node-5
checkout-5d7c8b6a4-g5h6i    1/1     Running   node-3

steps.prompt: The slow pods are the ones on node-3. During tonight's spike, see everything running on node-3 across all namespaces.
steps.fake_output:
NAMESPACE   NAME                              READY   STATUS
shop        checkout-5d7c8b6a4-a1b2c          1/1     Running
shop        checkout-5d7c8b6a4-g5h6i          1/1     Running
analytics   nightly-export-29311020-kx8zq     1/1     Running

steps.prompt: A nightly analytics CronJob pod shares the node. Check its CPU and memory usage in analytics.
It uses 7.8 of node-3's 8 cores. Check its resource settings.
expected_commands: kubectl get pod nightly-export-29311020-kx8zq -n analytics -o yaml | grep -A6 resources

steps.prompt: No requests or limits, so it can take the whole node. Stop it happening in that namespace at all: apply the LimitRange in analytics-limits.yaml to the analytics namespace, giving every container default requests and limits.

resolution: A classic noisy neighbour: a nightly batch job with no resource requests or limits, scheduled onto the same node as latency-sensitive checkout pods, took almost all the node's CPU for 40 minutes. The checkout pods on that node were CPU-starved, while those on other nodes were fine, which is why 'only some pods' and 'only at 01:00' were the key clues. Fixes, from immediate to structural: give the batch job requests and a CPU limit (the LimitRange now makes defaults mandatory in that namespace); use a ResourceQuota per team namespace; set PriorityClasses so batch work yields to user-facing work; and at scale, run batch on a separate node pool with taints, so it can't land next to checkout at all. Google's Borg paper describes the same idea: mixing batch and serving work on shared machines is efficient only if isolation is enforced.
